overview.text: Money is something people generally accept as final payment for goods and services. It has three main functions: serving as a medium of exchange, a unit of account for comparing prices, and a store of value that can be saved for later. These functions make trading easier than relying on barter, where each person must find someone willing to trade for exactly what they want. Money is not limited to coins and banknotes: examples across history include shells and stone wheels, while modern systems also use electronic bank deposits. Commodity money gets value from its material; fiat money is not redeemable for a commodity and relies on public acceptance. Inflation can reduce money’s purchasing power over time.

key_facts.text: As a medium of exchange, money is widely accepted as a way to pay; this helps people trade without arranging a direct barter of goods or services.
As a unit of account, money gives buyers and sellers a shared way to state and compare prices.
Money can store value for future spending, but it is not a perfect store: inflation can erode its purchasing power.
Commodity money has value from the material it is made of, such as gold; fiat money is not convertible into gold or another asset and depends on public trust and acceptance.
Money can be physical or digital: examples include coins and banknotes, commercial-bank deposits, and digital balances held at nonbank providers.
